title: Knitting a gauge swatch
subtitle: How to cast on, work, and measure a swatch before starting any project.
excerpt: A gauge swatch is a small knitted sample used to check that your stitches and rows match the numbers the pattern states. Ten minutes with a swatch can save a week of reworking.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 1 (1886), opening chapter on tension. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), pp. 18-22. Craft Yarn Council tension and swatch standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitted sample worked in the pattern stitch and yarn called for, used to measure tension before starting the main piece. UK knitting calls this a tension swatch.
The number of stitches and rows per 10 cm in a given stitch and yarn. UK term for what US patterns call gauge.

content.text: swatch) is a small sample knitted in the yarn and stitch the pattern calls for before the main piece begins. UK patterns state tension as stitches and rows per 10 cm. If your swatch matches those numbers, your finished piece will match the stated dimensions. If it does not, you adjust needle size until it does. Difficulty: beginner in execution, though it asks the knitter to slow down before casting on.
The yarn the pattern calls for
Needles in the size the pattern recommends (and one size up and one size down as backups)
Working the swatch, step by step
Cast on at least 30 stitches. More stitches give a wider sample and a more reliable reading.
Work in the stitch the pattern specifies (usually stocking stitch unless the pattern is an all-over texture) for at least 30 rows. This gives a tall enough swatch to count row tension accurately.
Cast off loosely. Block the swatch as you would the finished piece: wet-block a wool swatch, leave a cotton swatch unblocked unless the pattern calls otherwise.
Lay the swatch flat. Pin a marker at two points exactly 10 cm apart horizontally across the middle of the swatch, away from the cast-on and cast-off edges.
Count the stitches between the two pins. This is your stitch tension per 10 cm. Repeat vertically for row tension.
If you have more stitches than the pattern states, your tension is too tight: go up one needle size. If fewer, go down one size. Rework the swatch on the new needles and measure again.

Every UK knitting pattern lists a tension figure at the top of the page. Garment patterns and fitted accessories (hats, socks, mittens) depend on the swatch matching. Scarves and blankets where small size differences do not matter are the only common exception.

items.symptom: Swatch looks different from main fabric
items.cause: Not blocking the swatch, or using a different stitch
items.fix: Block the swatch the same way you will block the finished piece. Work it in the same stitch the pattern uses for the body, not in garter stitch.

items.symptom: Tension matches on stitches but not on rows
items.cause: Row and stitch tension are independent
items.fix: Garment length is usually adjustable by working more or fewer rows; width depends on stitch count. Match the stitch tension first. If row tension is off by one row per 10 cm on a scarf, the effect on length is small.

items.symptom: Tension changes between the swatch and the main piece
items.cause: Knitting in the round produces different tension from flat knitting for many people
items.fix: If the pattern is worked in the round, work the swatch in the round (knit a small tube rather than flat rows).
